title: No, this is ours. We have been deprived.
subtitle: The moment denial turns into the truth
then: Ibn Kathir says they changed their minds and {idea}realized it was the right path after all.{/idea} Then they said: {trap}this is it, but we have no portion and no share.{/trap} They had planned to deprive the poor. They were the ones deprived.
now: You held back from helping your sister with rent, and then the car broke down for the same amount. {trap}What you keep from others does not always stay with you.{/trap} {idea}Not as a rule to calculate, but as a reason to reflect.{/idea}
old: Holding back from others keeps more for me.
new: Depriving others can leave me the one deprived.
try: Think of someone you have been holding back from helping. Help them in one small way today.

title: The fairest brother said: did I not tell you?
subtitle: The one voice that tried to stop them

row.title: glorify Allah
sub: say if Allah wills, give thanks

then: The early scholars said the awsat was {reward}the most just and the best of them.{/reward} He had warned: why do you not glorify Allah? Mujahid said it meant {idea}why do you not say if Allah wills?{/idea} Others said it meant thank Allah for His favor.
now: There is usually one person in the group who says, maybe we should not. The colleague who asks if this is honest. The cousin who says, let us include them. {idea}Be glad of that voice. Or be that voice.{/idea}
old: The one who objects is just slowing everyone down.
new: The quiet voice reminding us of Allah is often the wisest one in the room.
try: Next time a group plan feels wrong, say one calm sentence about it.

title: Glory to our Lord. We were the wrongdoers.
subtitle: Admitting the wrong, though late

row.title: before the loss
sub: when it can still change things

then: They finally said what the best brother had asked for. Ibn Kathir notes {trap}they became obedient when it was of no benefit to the garden{/trap}, and confessed when it could not save it. Still, {idea}they named their wrong honestly.{/idea}
now: You apologize to your friend only after they stop answering. You start praying only when the hospital calls. {trap}Waking up late is still waking up.{/trap} {idea}But earlier is always better.{/idea}
old: I will fix things when something forces me to.
new: Saying I was wrong to Allah now is better than saying it after the loss.
try: Say one honest sentence to Allah today about a wrong you have not admitted yet.

title: Then they turned on each other with blame.
subtitle: After the loss, the finger pointing
then: Ibn Kathir says {trap}they started blaming each other{/trap} for what they had decided: keeping the poor from their right to the fruit. In the end their answer to one another was only to {idea}confess the error together.{/idea}
now: The project fails and the team chat fills with who said what. A family plan goes wrong and every sibling has a version. {trap}Blame feels like relief, but it fixes nothing.{/trap} {idea}Owning your part does.{/idea}
old: If I can show it was someone else's idea, I am clear.
new: If I went along with a wrong, I own my part of it.
try: Think of a recent group mistake. Say to one person: my part in it was this.

title: Woe to us. We went beyond every limit.
subtitle: Seeing how far you crossed the line

key.label: How it felt vs what it was

then: Ibn Kathir explains they meant: {trap}we transgressed, trespassed and exceeded the bounds{/trap} until this happened to us. What felt like a smart plan the night before {idea}now looked like what it really was.{/idea}
now: At the time it was just one small shortcut on the tax form, one harsh word to your child. Later you see it whole. {trap}Limits are often crossed one step at a time.{/trap} {idea}Seeing it clearly is the start of coming back.{/idea}
old: It was only a small step over the line.
new: Small crossings add up, and naming them honestly opens the way back.
try: Name one line you have been slowly crossing. Step back from it once today.

title: Perhaps our Lord will give us something better.
subtitle: Hope right after the loss

row.title: hope in Allah
sub: He can replace it with better

then: The story ends with the brothers {reward}turning to their Lord in hope.{/reward} Ibn Kathir says some said they hoped for {reward}a better garden in this life{/reward}, others said for its reward in the Hereafter. And Allah knows best.
now: You lost the job, the deal, the friendship, and part of it was your fault. The voice in your head says it is over. {reward}The door to Allah is still open.{/reward} {idea}Regret that turns to hope is the right kind.{/idea}
old: I messed up. There is no coming back from this.
new: After a loss I caused, I can still turn to Allah and hope for better.
try: Make one du'a today asking Allah to replace something you lost with something better.

title: This is the worldly loss. The next one is greater.
subtitle: The parable's lesson for everyone listening
then: Ibn Kathir says {trap}such is the punishment of whoever opposes Allah's command and is stingy{/trap} with what Allah gave him. The surah introduction says Makkah was being told: {idea}you too have been tested like the garden owners.{/idea}
now: Losing money hurts. Losing a business hurts more. {trap}But some losses are bigger than anything on a bank statement.{/trap} {idea}The story is told so you can choose differently while there is time.{/idea}
old: The worst thing that can happen is losing what I have here.
new: Worldly loss is a warning. What truly matters is the Hereafter.
try: Give something today from what you love most, as a small step for the Hereafter.

title: The mindful have gardens with their Lord that never wither.
subtitle: The other garden, after the lost one
then: Right after the garden that was destroyed, Allah mentions another. Ibn Kathir says those with taqwa {reward}will have Gardens of Delight in the Hereafter that will never end{/reward}, and {reward}their pleasures will never cease.{/reward}
now: You scroll past homes, holidays, gardens that seem perfect. All of them can vanish in a night. {reward}There is a garden that will not.{/reward} {idea}It is built by being mindful of Allah.{/idea}
old: The good life is the one I can see and touch now.
new: The garden that lasts is with Allah, and taqwa is how I reach it.
try: Do one act today purely out of mindfulness of Allah, with the lasting garden in mind.

title: Would Allah treat the obedient and the criminals the same?
subtitle: Justice means different outcomes for different paths

row.title: surely not
sub: by the Lord of heaven and earth

then: The chiefs of Makkah assumed they would do fine whatever happened. Ibn Kathir explains the question: {idea}should We deal equally between them in recompense?{/idea} His answer: {trap}nay, surely not.{/trap}
now: The honest worker and the one who cheats get the same bonus. The kind sibling and the cruel one get the same praise. {trap}It can feel like goodness does not count.{/trap} {idea}With Allah, it always counts.{/idea}
old: Good or bad, it all ends up the same in the end.
new: Allah is just. Obedience and wrongdoing do not end in the same place.
try: Do one good deed today that nobody will reward you for, trusting that Allah sees it.

title: What is wrong with you? How can you judge this way?
subtitle: Questioning a comfortable assumption
then: After asking if the obedient and the criminals are equal, Allah asks the deniers directly: what is the matter with you? Ibn Kathir explains: {idea}how can you think that?{/idea} {trap}Their confidence had no ground.{/trap}
now: I am a good person, I will be fine. You hear it, and maybe you say it. {trap}A feeling dressed as a certainty.{/trap} {idea}The verse asks: on what basis?{/idea}
old: I am basically good, so I do not need to worry.
new: My hopes about the Hereafter need a real basis, not just a feeling.
try: Write down one assumption you have about your standing with Allah. Ask what it rests on.

title: Do you have a scripture that says you can do anything?
subtitle: Asking for the source of a claim
then: Ibn Kathir explains Allah is asking: {idea}is there in your hands a Book sent from heaven{/idea} that you study and memorize and pass on through the generations, {trap}containing the laws you claim?{/trap} They had nothing of the kind.
now: It is fine, everyone does it. Allah will understand. You make up a rule because it suits you. {trap}A private scripture written by your wishes.{/trap} {idea}The question is fair: where does it say that?{/idea}
old: I know Allah would be fine with this.
new: If I claim something about Allah, I should be able to show where it comes from.
try: Pick one religious thing you say often. Check its source this week.

title: A book promising you whatever you choose?
subtitle: The fantasy of getting everything you want
then: The challenge continues: does your book say {trap}you shall have all that you choose?{/trap} The chiefs acted as if {trap}their wishes were guaranteed.{/trap} Ibn Kathir shows there was no such book.
now: Some ads promise that you deserve it all. Some talks promise that if you want it enough, it is yours. {trap}A world where wanting equals having.{/trap} {idea}The Hereafter does not work by wishes.{/idea}
old: If I want it badly enough, I will get it.
new: My outcome is not what I choose but what Allah judges by my deeds.
try: Replace one I deserve thought today with I hope, Allah willing.

title: Did Allah swear an oath to give you what you decide?
subtitle: No one holds a contract over Allah
then: Ibn Kathir explains: {trap}do you have covenants and confirmed agreements with Us{/trap}, that you will attain all you want and desire? The chiefs acted as if Allah had signed a deal with them. {idea}He had not.{/idea}
now: I pray, so my business should succeed. I fasted, so my exam should go well. {trap}Quietly turning worship into a contract.{/trap} {idea}Allah is generous, but He is not bound to my terms.{/idea}
old: I have done my part, so Allah has to give me what I asked.
new: Allah owes me nothing. Everything He gives is generosity.
try: Make one du'a today that ends with: but You know what is best for me.
